title: Introduction
text:
Why put an app in a package?
This section will introduce the main resources the book is built around, how to set up Python development tools on your local machine, and common integrated development environments (IDEs) for Shiny for Python applications.
A standalone app.py file is a fine place to start. But as an app grows, packaging it offers real benefits:

title: Introduction
text:
Reusability: share utility functions, modules, and data across projects

Testability: pytest can test code that lives in an importable package
Reproducibility: pyproject.toml files make dependencies explicit and installable

Deployability: properly packaged apps are easier to containerize and deploy

title: Introduction
text:
Primary resources
This section will introduce the main resources the book is built around: Shiny for Python, Python packages, and the Python Packaging User Guide.

Shiny for Python
We’re going to be using the application and code referenced directly from Posit’s documentation: https://shiny.posit.co/py/
You’ll notice Shiny for Python has two syntax modes, express and core.


Python Packages
The Python Packages book is an excellent resource for understanding how to package a Python project. It’s also written in the same basic style and structure of R Packages, 2ed, so if you’re coming from the R development world (as I am), these similarities should be comforting.


Python Packaging User Guide
The Python Packaging User Guide is the official reference for packaging Python projects, maintained by the Python Packaging Authority (PyPA). When a tool or file format in this book needs a more authoritative explanation (like pyproject.toml, build backends, or publishing to PyPI), this is where I’ll point you.

title: Introduction
text:
System setup
The sections below cover the technologies we’ll be using in the book. I primarily develop on MacBook Pro (with macOS), but also use a System76 laptop, which uses an Ubuntu-flavored operating system. I’ve tried to keep the examples general enough that most readers will be able to follow along, regardless of their operating system.

Terminals
Terminals are a command-line interface (CLI) for communicating with your computer. This includes the macOS Terminal, or the WSL for Windows. You can also download terminal emulators (like iTerm2), which offer a lot more options for customizing your CLI experience.


Python installations
The examples in this book use Python 3.12. Most macOS and Ubuntu machines already come with a system Python (the version the operating system depends on), but I recommend leaving it alone and installing a separate Python for development. You can download installers for macOS and Windows from python.org, but I’ve found it easier to let uv (covered in the next section) install and manage Python versions for me.
After installing uv, the commands below install Python 3.12 and list the Python versions uv can find on your machine. They work the same in the macOS/Ubuntu terminal and Windows PowerShell:
uv python install 3.12
uv python list
If you’ve used rig to install and switch between R versions, uv python fills the same role.


Python packaging software
R developers get most of their package development toolchain from devtools, usethis, and renv. Python splits these jobs across several tools (pip, venv, setuptools, hatch, poetry, and others), which can be confusing when you’re first starting out. This book uses uv, a single command-line tool that installs Python versions, creates virtual environments, installs packages, and records exact versions in a lockfile.
Install uv on macOS or Ubuntu with the standalone installer:
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
On Windows, run the installer from PowerShell:
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
The table below maps the uv commands we’ll use most often to their closest R equivalents:



Task
R
Python (uv)

Create a package

Add a dependency

Package metadata and dependencies live in pyproject.toml, which is Python’s version of the DESCRIPTION file. The early branches of pyap install dependencies from a requirements.txt file with uv pip install, and later branches move to pyproject.toml, uv add, and uv.lock. If you’d rather not install uv, Python’s built-in venv and pip cover the essentials, and the Shiny for Python chapter shows the equivalent commands.

title: 1  Whole Game
text:
1.1 The starting app
This chapter walks through the complete workflow, from a bare app.py to a working app inside an installable package. It’s modeled on the Whole Game chapter of R Packages, 2ed.
I’ll touch on each area of the development workflow used throughout the rest of the book, so you can see how the pieces fit together before we cover each topic in detail.
We’ll start with a single app.py file stored in the pyap repository. The app simulates the Old Faithful geyser waiting times and displays them in a histogram, with a slider that controls the number of bins:
The app uses the Shiny Core API: app_ui defines the layout, server() defines the outputs, and App() combines them into the app object. The Shiny for Python chapter covers each of these components in detail.

title: 1  Whole Game
text:
# This is a Shiny for Python application.
# Run it with: shiny run app.py

from shiny import App, ui, render
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

# Old Faithful geyser waiting time data (bimodal distribution)
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
waiting = np.concatenate([
    rng.normal(54, 5, 100),   # short-wait eruption cluster
    rng.normal(80, 6, 172),   # long-wait eruption cluster
])

app_ui = ui.page_sidebar(
    ui.sidebar(
        ui.input_slider(
            "bins",
            "Number of bins:",
            min=1,
            max=50,
            value=30,
        ),
    ),
    ui.output_plot("distPlot"),
    title="Old Faithful Geyser Data",
)


def server(input, output, session):
    @render.plot
    def distPlot():
        fig, ax = plt.subplots()
        ax.hist(waiting, bins=input.bins(), color="darkgray", edgecolor="white")
        ax.set_xlabel("Waiting time to next eruption (in mins)")
        ax.set_title("Histogram of waiting times")
        return fig


app = App(app_ui, server)

title: 1  Whole Game
text:
1.2 Create the project
The first step is turning the folder that holds app.py into a uv project. From inside that folder, uv init --package creates the package scaffolding, and --python 3.12 pins the Python version we’re using in this book:1
cd pyap
uv init --package --python 3.12

Initialized project `pyap`

uv takes the project name from the folder name, so the package is named pyap. The folder now looks like this:

pyap/
├── .python-version
├── README.md
├── app.py
├── pyproject.toml
└── src/
    └── pyap/
        └── __init__.py

.python-version records the Python version uv will use for the project, and src/pyap/ is the importable package. uv won’t overwrite an existing README.md. If the folder isn’t already a Git repository, uv init also runs git init and writes a .gitignore (we’ll come back to Git at the end of the chapter).

title: 1  Whole Game
text:
1.3 Package metadata
Every Python package needs a pyproject.toml file. This is where the package name, version, description, authors, dependencies, and build settings live.2 The file uv init --package created is shown below:
[project]
name = "pyap"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Add your description here"
readme = "README.md"
authors = [
    { name = "Jane Doe", email = "jane.doe@email.io" }
]
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = []

[project.scripts]
pyap = "pyap:main"

[build-system]
requires = ["uv_build>=0.12.23,<0.13.0"]
build-backend = "uv_build"
uv fills in authors from your Git configuration, and the version range under [build-system] depends on which version of uv you have installed. The [project.scripts] table registers a terminal command (we’ll replace it when we add a launch function below).
The only field we’ll edit right now is description:
description = "A Shiny for Python app-package"
The Python Packages chapter covers the rest of the fields in pyproject.toml.

title: 1  Whole Game
section: 1.4 Move the app into the package
text:
1.4 Move the app into the package
Code in a package lives inside the package directory, so we’ll move app.py into src/pyap/:
mv app.py src/pyap/app.py

pyap/
├── .python-version
├── README.md
├── pyproject.toml
└── src/
    └── pyap/
        ├── __init__.py
        └── app.py

Keeping the package under src/ means Python can only import pyap after it’s installed. This sounds like a restriction, but it guarantees our tests run against the installed package (not whatever files happen to be in the working directory). The src/ Layout chapter explains why this matters.

title: 1  Whole Game
text:
1.5 Add dependencies
app.py imports shiny, matplotlib, and numpy, so all three need to be listed as package dependencies. uv add records them in pyproject.toml and installs them in one step:
uv add matplotlib numpy shiny
The dependencies field in pyproject.toml now lists each package with a lower version bound (your versions will match whatever was current when you ran the command):
dependencies = [
    "matplotlib>=3.11.2",
    "numpy>=2.5.3",
    "shiny>=1.8.0",
]
The first uv add also creates two new items in the project folder. .venv/ is the project’s virtual environment, and uv.lock records the exact version of every package installed in it. The Dependencies chapter covers how to declare, pin, and update dependencies.

title: 1  Whole Game
text:
1.6 Install in editable mode
uv installs the project itself into .venv/ whenever it syncs the environment, and it uses an editable install by default. An editable install points Python at the files in src/pyap/ instead of copying them, so any changes we make to the package are available the next time it’s imported (without reinstalling).3
uv add already synced the environment, but we can run uv sync any time to bring .venv/ in line with pyproject.toml and uv.lock:
uv sync
We can verify pyap is installed (and points to our source files) by importing it with uv run, which runs a command inside the project’s environment without activating it first:
uv run python -c "import pyap; print(pyap.__file__)"

/path/to/pyap/src/pyap/__init__.py







TipPositron



Positron detects the .venv/ folder in the project. Select it from the interpreter picker so the console, the editor, and the test runner all use the same environment as uv run.


The Development Workflow chapter covers the edit, sync, and run loop in more detail.

title: 1  Whole Game
text:
1.7 Run the app
With the dependencies installed, we can launch the app from its new location. The --reload flag restarts the app whenever we save a change to the code, and --launch-browser opens it in a browser:
uv run shiny run --reload --launch-browser src/pyap/app.py
The app looks exactly the same as it did before we moved it. Press Ctrl + C in the terminal to stop it.

title: 1  Whole Game
text:
1.8 Add a function
Right now the data are created at the top of app.py, which makes them hard to reuse or test. We’ll move that code into a function in a new module, src/pyap/data.py:
"""Data for the pyap app."""

import numpy as np


def geyser_waiting(seed: int = 42) -> np.ndarray:
    """Simulate Old Faithful geyser waiting times.

    Draws from two normal distributions (short and long waits) to
    mimic the bimodal shape of the original geyser data.

    Args:
        seed: Seed for the random number generator.

    Returns:
        A 1D array of 272 waiting times (in minutes).
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    return np.concatenate([
        rng.normal(54, 5, 100),
        rng.normal(80, 6, 172),
    ])
In src/pyap/app.py, we’ll replace the numpy import and the data code with a call to the new function:
from shiny import App, ui, render
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from pyap.data import geyser_waiting

waiting = geyser_waiting()
The import uses the full package path (pyap.data), which works because pyap is installed in editable mode. If the app is still running with --reload, saving both files should restart it with the same histogram.

title: 1  Whole Game
text:
1.9 Document
The text between the triple quotes in geyser_waiting() is a docstring. Docstrings are the primary way to document Python code, and they’re stored on the object itself, so there’s no separate step to generate help files.4 We can read it in the Python console:
>>> from pyap.data import geyser_waiting
>>> help(geyser_waiting)
The docstring above follows the Google style (Args: and Returns: sections). The Documentation chapter covers docstring conventions and how to build a documentation site from them.

title: 1  Whole Game
text:
1.10 Test
pytest is the most common Python testing framework. We only need it while developing the package (not when running the app), so we’ll add it to the dev dependency group with --dev:
uv add --dev pytest
[dependency-groups]
dev = [
    "pytest>=9.1.1",
]
Tests go in a tests/ folder at the root of the project, in files whose names start with test_. The tests below check that geyser_waiting() returns the expected number of values and that the same seed always produces the same data. We’ll save them in tests/test_data.py:
import numpy as np

from pyap.data import geyser_waiting


def test_geyser_waiting_length():
    assert len(geyser_waiting()) == 272


def test_geyser_waiting_reproducible():
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(geyser_waiting(seed=1), geyser_waiting(seed=1))
uv run pytest finds and runs every test in tests/:
uv run pytest
The output (trimmed) tells us both tests passed:

collected 2 items

tests/test_data.py ..                                                    [100%]

============================== 2 passed in 0.15s ===============================

The Test Suite chapter covers configuring pytest and running tests in Positron, and the rest of the Testing section covers fixtures, module tests, and end-to-end tests.

title: 1  Whole Game
text:
1.11 Add a launch function
Users of our package shouldn’t need to know the path to app.py to run the app. We’ll add run_app to the shiny import at the top of src/pyap/app.py, then add a run() function at the bottom of the file that calls it:
from shiny import App, ui, render, run_app

# ... app_ui, server(), and app are unchanged ...


def run() -> None:
    """Launch the pyap Shiny app in a browser."""
    run_app("pyap.app:app", launch_browser=True)
The "pyap.app:app" string tells Shiny to import the app object from the pyap.app module.
Next we’ll register run() as a terminal command by replacing the [project.scripts] entry uv init created:
[project.scripts]
pyap = "pyap.app:run"
The original entry pointed to a placeholder main() function in src/pyap/__init__.py. Nothing refers to it anymore, so we can replace the contents of __init__.py with a one-line docstring:
"""A Shiny for Python app-package."""
After syncing the environment, the pyap command launches the app:
uv sync
uv run pyap
We can also launch the app from the Python console with from pyap.app import run and run(). The Launch chapter covers entry points in more detail (including running the package with python -m pyap, which requires a src/pyap/__main__.py file containing from pyap.app import run; run()).

title: 1  Whole Game
text:
1.12 Build
uv build packages the project into a source distribution and a wheel (a pre-built, installable archive) in a new dist/ folder:
uv build

dist/
├── pyap-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
└── pyap-0.1.0.tar.gz

The wheel is the installable package. Anyone with Python 3.12 or later can install it (along with shiny, matplotlib, and numpy) and launch the app with the pyap command:
pip install dist/pyap-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl
pyap
The PyPI chapter covers publishing the package so it can be installed by name.

text:
1.13 README
The README.md is the first thing users and contributors see in the repository, so it should explain what the package does and how to install and run it. A minimal version for pyap is below:

A Shiny for Python app-package.

## Installation

```bash
pip install git+https://github.com/<username>/pyap.git
```

title: 1  Whole Game
text:
1.14 Git and GitHub
The last step is committing the project to Git. Because pyap is already a Git repository, uv doesn’t generate a .gitignore, so make sure yours lists the virtual environment (.venv/), dist/, and Python cache files (__pycache__/) before committing everything else:
git add .
git commit -m "Create pyap app-package"
uv.lock should be committed with the rest of the project. It guarantees everyone who runs uv sync gets the exact same package versions.
If you have the GitHub CLI installed, gh repo create creates the repository on GitHub and pushes the local commits in one step:
gh repo create pyap --public --source=. --push
The GitHub Setup appendix covers creating the repository, configuring .gitignore, and protecting the main branch.

title: 1  Whole Game
text:
1.15 Recap
In this chapter we turned a single app.py file into an installable Python package. The final project is shown below:

pyap/
├── .gitignore
├── .python-version
├── .venv/
├── README.md
├── dist/
├── pyproject.toml
├── src/
│   └── pyap/
│       ├── __init__.py
│       ├── app.py
│       └── data.py
├── tests/
│   └── test_data.py
└── uv.lock

The workflow followed these steps:

Create the project with uv init --package and edit the metadata in pyproject.toml.
Move app.py into the src/pyap/ package.
Add dependencies with uv add (which also installs the package in editable mode).
Move code into documented functions, then test them with pytest.
Add a launch function and register it as a command under [project.scripts].
Build the package with uv build, write a README.md, and commit the project to Git.

The rest of the book covers each of these steps in detail, starting with the Shiny for Python chapter.

2.2 Virtual environments
In Python, it’s a good idea to use a virtual environment. This practice might be new to R developers, so I’ll give a quick overview.1

2.2.1 How virtual environments work
Python virtual environments isolate a project’s dependencies, so any packages installed for one project don’t conflict with other projects. Two common tools used in this approach are illustrated below:

 Python built-in virtual environments 



Python’s built-in virtual environment tool (venv) ships with Python. The general workflow is:

Create virtual environment (python -m venv)

Use the environment (activate)

Install dependencies (pip install)

venv doesn’t have a built-in lockfile, which also means we’ll need to also run pip freeze to store the dependencies in requirements.txt.

uv requires a separate install command, 2 but also includes a global cache with hardlinks. During installation, uv reuses downloaded dependencies across projects, which is typically faster than copying/downloading them each time (as venv does). uv add also installs new dependencies in one step, and the uv.lock file automatically tracks exact versions.
Both tools create a .venv/ folder with an isolated Python interpreter and its own site-packages/ directory. When activated, the shell points to that Python instead of the System Python. So, pip install shiny only installs shiny in this project.


2.2.2 Virtual environment setup
Install uv with:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

uv venv
If you don’t want to install/use uv, you can use Python’s built-in venv:
python -m venv .venv

source .venv/bin/activate
The terminal prompt will prepend with (pyap).

.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

title: 2  Shiny for Python
text:
2.3 Hello Shiny
The first app in this chapter is the Old Faithful histogram we saw at the start of the Whole Game chapter. In the Whole Game, we moved this app into a package without looking closely at how it works. Here we’ll slow down and walk through each piece of the Core API.
If you’re following along with the pyap repository, check out the 02.1_shiny-app branch:
git checkout 02.1_shiny-app
The branch contains a single app.py file (along with a README.md and a .gitignore). The app imports matplotlib and numpy in addition to shiny, so we’ll install both into the virtual environment before running it:
uv pip install matplotlib numpy
The .venv/ folder isn’t tracked by Git, so the same virtual environment stays in place when we switch branches. Each time we check out a new branch, we install whatever new packages that branch needs (the chapter will point these out).

2.3.1 app.py
The full contents of app.py are below:
# This is a Shiny for Python application.
# Run it with: shiny run app.py

from shiny import App, ui, render
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

# Old Faithful geyser waiting time data (bimodal distribution)
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
waiting = np.concatenate([
    rng.normal(54, 5, 100),   # short-wait eruption cluster
    rng.normal(80, 6, 172),   # long-wait eruption cluster
])

app_ui = ui.page_sidebar(
    ui.sidebar(
        ui.input_slider(
            "bins",
            "Number of bins:",
            min=1,
            max=50,
            value=30,
        ),
    ),
    ui.output_plot("distPlot"),
    title="Old Faithful Geyser Data",
)


def server(input, output, session):
    @render.plot
    def distPlot():
        fig, ax = plt.subplots()
        ax.hist(waiting, bins=input.bins(), color="darkgray", edgecolor="white")
        ax.set_xlabel("Waiting time to next eruption (in mins)")
        ax.set_title("Histogram of waiting times")
        return fig


app = App(app_ui, server)
Every Core API app is built from the same three parts: a UI object, a server function, and a call to App() that combines them. The waiting data are created at the top of the file (outside the server), so they’re computed once when the app starts rather than each time the plot is drawn.


2.3.2 Imports
The first line imports the three Core API components we’ll use from shiny:
from shiny import App, ui, render
ui holds the functions for building the layout, inputs, and outputs. render holds the decorators that turn Python functions into outputs, and App is the class that builds the application object.


2.3.3 UI
The UI is a nested set of function calls stored in app_ui. ui.page_sidebar() creates a page with a sidebar on the left and a main content area on the right:
app_ui = ui.page_sidebar(
    ui.sidebar(
        ui.input_slider(
            "bins",
            "Number of bins:",
            min=1,
            max=50,
            value=30,
        ),
    ),
    ui.output_plot("distPlot"),
    title="Old Faithful Geyser Data",
)
The first argument to ui.page_sidebar() is the ui.sidebar(), and everything after it goes in the main area. The sidebar holds a single slider input, ui.input_slider(), which takes an id ("bins"), a label, and the min, max, and starting value. The main area holds ui.output_plot(), which reserves space for a plot with the id "distPlot".
These two ids are how the UI and server find each other. The server reads the slider value using "bins", and it sends the plot back to the space reserved by "distPlot".


2.3.4 Server
The server is a function that Shiny calls once for each user session. It takes three arguments: input, output, and session:
def server(input, output, session):
    @render.plot
    def distPlot():
        fig, ax = plt.subplots()
        ax.hist(waiting, bins=input.bins(), color="darkgray", edgecolor="white")
        ax.set_xlabel("Waiting time to next eruption (in mins)")
        ax.set_title("Histogram of waiting times")
        return fig
Outputs are defined as functions inside the server. The @render.plot line is a decorator, a function that wraps the function defined below it. In this case, it tells Shiny that distPlot() returns a plot. The function name is the output id, so distPlot() fills the space created by ui.output_plot("distPlot") in the UI.3
Inside distPlot(), the slider value is read with input.bins(). Inputs are reactive values, so we call them like functions to get their current value.4 Reading input.bins() inside a render function also creates a reactive dependency: whenever the slider moves, Shiny re-runs distPlot() and redraws the histogram. The function builds the histogram with matplotlib and returns the figure, which @render.plot displays in the app.
We don’t use output or session in this app, but we’ll see them again when we cover modules and reactive patterns in later chapters.


2.3.5 App
The last line combines the UI and server into a Shiny application:5
app = App(app_ui, server)
The name of this object matters. When we run the app, Shiny looks for an object named app in app.py by default.


2.3.6 Run the app
With the virtual environment activated, we can launch the app from the terminal with shiny run:
shiny run app.py
Shiny starts a local web server and prints its address in the terminal (http://127.0.0.1:8000 by default). Open the address in a browser to view the app, and move the slider to confirm the histogram updates with the number of bins.
During development, the same --reload and --launch-browser flags we used in the Whole Game chapter restart the app whenever we save a change and open it in a browser automatically:
shiny run --reload --launch-browser app.py
Press Ctrl + C in the terminal to stop the app.

title: 2  Shiny for Python
text:
2.4 Movies app
The Old Faithful app is a good introduction, but it’s too small to show the problems that come up as an app grows. The app we’ll use for the rest of the book is a scatter plot of movie review data, and it has more inputs, a helper function in a separate file, and a dataset that’s read from disk. The code and data come from the Building Web Applications with Shiny course.
Check out the 02.2_movies-app branch to follow along:
git checkout 02.2_movies-app
The branch replaces the Old Faithful code with three files:

pyap/
├── app.py
├── movies.csv
└── utils.py

The movies app reads the data with pandas, so we’ll install it into the virtual environment (shiny and matplotlib are already installed):
uv pip install pandas






Notepandas or polars?





This book uses pandas because it’s more common in Shiny for Python examples (roughly 3 to 1 over polars in the py-shiny and py-shiny-templates repositories as of 2026-10). Shiny doesn’t force the choice, though: @render.data_frame accepts both pandas and polars DataFrames. To follow along with polars instead, install it into the virtual environment:
uv pip install polars
polars builds queries from column expressions (like pl.col("genre")), so its syntax will feel familiar if you’re coming from dplyr.




2.4.1 app.py
The full app.py for the movies app is below:
# Run with: shiny run app.py
from shiny import App, ui, render, reactive
import pandas as pd
from utils import scatter_plot

movies = pd.read_csv("movies.csv")

app_ui = ui.page_sidebar(
    ui.sidebar(
        ui.input_select(
            "y",
            "Y-axis:",
            choices={
                "imdb_rating": "IMDB rating",
                "imdb_num_votes": "IMDB number of votes",
                "critics_score": "Critics Score",
                "audience_score": "Audience Score",
                "runtime": "Runtime",
            },
            selected="audience_score",
        ),
        ui.input_select(
            "x",
            "X-axis:",
            choices={
                "imdb_rating": "IMDB rating",
                "imdb_num_votes": "IMDB number of votes",
                "critics_score": "Critics Score",
                "audience_score": "Audience Score",
                "runtime": "Runtime",
            },
            selected="critics_score",
        ),
        ui.input_select(
            "z",
            "Color by:",
            choices={
                "title_type": "Title Type",
                "genre": "Genre",
                "mpaa_rating": "MPAA Rating",
                "critics_rating": "Critics Rating",
                "audience_rating": "Audience Rating",
            },
            selected="mpaa_rating",
        ),
        ui.input_slider(
            "alpha", "Alpha:", min=0.0, max=1.0, value=0.4, step=0.05
        ),
        ui.input_slider("size", "Size:", min=1, max=5, value=3),
        ui.input_text(
            "plot_title",
            "Plot title",
            placeholder="Enter text to be used as plot title",
        ),
        ui.input_action_button("update_plot_title", "Update plot title"),
    ),
    ui.p(
        "These data were obtained from ",
        ui.a("IMDB", href="http://www.imdb.com/"),
        " and ",
        ui.a("Rotten Tomatoes", href="https://www.rottentomatoes.com/"),
        ".",
    ),
    ui.p(
        f"The data represent {len(movies)} randomly sampled movies "
        "released between 1972 to 2014 in the United States."
    ),
    ui.output_plot("scatterplot"),
    ui.hr(),
    ui.p(
        ui.em(
            "The code for this Shiny application comes from ",
            ui.a(
                "Building Web Applications with Shiny",
                href="https://rstudio-education.github.io/shiny-course/",
            ),
        )
    ),
)


def server(input, output, session):
    # only updates title when button is clicked, runs on init with empty string
    @reactive.calc
    @reactive.event(input.update_plot_title, ignore_none=False, ignore_init=False)
    def new_plot_title():
        return input.plot_title().title()

    @render.plot
    def scatterplot():
        return scatter_plot(
            df=movies,
            x_var=input.x(),
            y_var=input.y(),
            col_var=input.z(),
            alpha_var=input.alpha(),
            size_var=input.size(),
            title=new_plot_title(),
        )


app = App(app_ui, server)
The structure is the same as the Old Faithful app: imports, a UI object, a server function, and App(). The differences are in what each part contains, so we’ll focus on those below.


2.4.2 Reading data
The app reads movies.csv into a pandas DataFrame (a table of rows and named columns) at the top of the file:
movies = pd.read_csv("movies.csv")
Like waiting in the Old Faithful app, movies is created outside the server, so the file is read once when the app starts and every session shares the same data. The path is relative, which means Python looks for movies.csv in the current working directory. We need to run the app from the folder that holds movies.csv (we’ll fix this fragile path when we store the data inside the package in the Data chapter).
The data have 34 columns describing each movie (title, genre, runtime, mpaa_rating, imdb_rating, critics_score, audience_score, and others). The app only plots a handful of them.






NoteReading data with polars





The code blocks below import the package, read movies.csv, and count rows in pandas, polars, and the tidyverse:
pandas:
import pandas as pd

movies = pd.read_csv("movies.csv")
len(movies)
polars:
import polars as pl

movies = pl.read_csv("movies.csv", null_values="NA")
len(movies)
R (tidyverse):
library(readr)

movies <- read_csv("movies.csv")
nrow(movies)
pandas reads the string NA as a missing value by default, but polars only treats empty fields as missing. Because movies.csv stores missing values as NA, pl.read_csv("movies.csv") fails with a parsing error, so we pass the string to null_values.





2.4.3 Inputs
The sidebar holds seven inputs. Three of them are ui.input_select() dropdowns for the x axis, the y axis, and the color variable. Each dropdown takes a choices dictionary, where the keys are the values sent to the server and the values are the labels displayed in the app:6
ui.input_select(
    "y",
    "Y-axis:",
    choices={
        "imdb_rating": "IMDB rating",
        "imdb_num_votes": "IMDB number of votes",
        "critics_score": "Critics Score",
        "audience_score": "Audience Score",
        "runtime": "Runtime",
    },
    selected="audience_score",
),
When a user picks “Critics Score” from the dropdown, input.y() returns "critics_score", which is the column name we need for the plot. selected sets the starting value.
The two ui.input_slider() calls control the transparency (alpha) and size of the points. The alpha slider uses step=0.05 to move in small increments between 0.0 and 1.0.
The last two inputs work together. ui.input_text() creates a text box for the plot title, and ui.input_action_button() creates a button that applies it. We’ll see how the server connects them below.


2.4.4 UI text
The main area holds more than the plot output. ui.p(), ui.a(), ui.em(), and ui.hr() create HTML paragraph, link, emphasis, and horizontal rule tags. Positional arguments become the tag’s contents, and keyword arguments (like href) become its attributes:
ui.p(
    "These data were obtained from ",
    ui.a("IMDB", href="http://www.imdb.com/"),
    " and ",
    ui.a("Rotten Tomatoes", href="https://www.rottentomatoes.com/"),
    ".",
),
The second paragraph uses an f-string to insert the number of rows in movies with len(movies). Because the UI is built once when the app starts, this number is computed once too (it isn’t reactive).


2.4.5 Reactive outputs
The server has two functions. scatterplot() is the output, and it follows the same pattern as distPlot() in the Old Faithful app: the @render.plot decorator, a function name that matches the ui.output_plot("scatterplot") id, and calls to input.x(), input.y(), and the other inputs. Each input read inside scatterplot() is a reactive dependency, so changing any dropdown or slider redraws the plot.
The plot title works differently. We don’t want the title to change with every keystroke in the text box, only when the button is clicked. new_plot_title() handles this with two decorators from the reactive module:
@reactive.calc
@reactive.event(input.update_plot_title, ignore_none=False, ignore_init=False)
def new_plot_title():
    return input.plot_title().title()
Decorators are applied from the bottom up, so we’ll read them in that order:

@reactive.event() limits when the function runs. It only responds to input.update_plot_title (the button), and it ignores changes to input.plot_title() even though the function reads it.
ignore_none=False and ignore_init=False let the function run once when the app starts (before the button has been clicked), so the first plot is drawn with an empty title instead of waiting for a click.
@reactive.calc turns the function into a reactive calculation, which caches its result and returns it to any output that calls new_plot_title().7

.title() is a Python string method that capitalizes the first letter of each word, so typing critics vs audience and clicking the button gives the plot the title “Critics Vs Audience”. scatterplot() calls new_plot_title() just like an input, which makes the reactive calculation one of its dependencies.


2.4.6 Utility functions
app.py doesn’t build the plot itself. The plotting code lives in scatter_plot(), a function in utils.py:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd


def scatter_plot(df, x_var, y_var, col_var, alpha_var, size_var, title=""):
    """Create a scatter plot of df colored by a categorical variable."""
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    categories = sorted(df[col_var].dropna().unique())
    cmap = plt.get_cmap("tab10")
    for i, cat in enumerate(categories):
        subset = df[df[col_var] == cat]
        ax.scatter(
            subset[x_var],
            subset[y_var],
            alpha=alpha_var,
            s=size_var ** 2 * 10,
            color=cmap(i % 10),
            label=str(cat),
        )
    ax.set_xlabel(x_var.replace("_", " ").title())
    ax.set_ylabel(y_var.replace("_", " ").title())
    if title:
        ax.set_title(title)
    ax.legend(
        title=col_var.replace("_", " ").title(),
        bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, 1),
        loc="upper left",
    )
    plt.tight_layout()
    return fig
matplotlib doesn’t map a categorical variable to colors automatically, so scatter_plot() loops over each category in col_var and draws its points with a color from the tab10 palette. The s argument sets the marker area, so size_var ** 2 * 10 scales the slider’s 1 to 5 range into visible point sizes. The axis and legend labels are built from the column names (critics_score becomes “Critics Score”), and the legend is placed outside the plot area so it doesn’t cover any points.






NoteFiltering with polars





The code blocks below show the two pandas operations in scatter_plot() next to their polars and dplyr equivalents (selecting the rows in a category, and the unique values with no missing entries):
pandas:
df[df[col_var] == cat]
df[col_var].dropna().unique()
polars:
df.filter(pl.col(col_var) == cat)
df[col_var].drop_nulls().unique()
R (dplyr):
filter(df, .data[[col_var]] == cat)
unique(na.omit(df[[col_var]]))
pl.col(col_var) refers to a column by name inside an expression, much like .data[[col_var]] in dplyr. Using it requires import polars as pl at the top of utils.py. polars doesn’t preserve the order of unique() results by default, but scatter_plot() already wraps them in sorted().



Moving this code out of app.py keeps the server short, and it gives us a plain Python function we can call (and test) without running the app. app.py imports it with from utils import scatter_plot, which works because utils.py sits in the same folder as app.py. This is the same idea behind the geyser_waiting() function we added in the Whole Game chapter, and it’s where the package structure in later chapters starts to pay off.


2.4.7 Run the movies app
We launch the movies app the same way we launched the Old Faithful app, from the folder that holds app.py and movies.csv:
shiny run --reload --launch-browser app.py
We can confirm the app is working by changing the x axis, y axis, and color dropdowns and watching the scatter plot update. Typing a title in the text box should leave the plot unchanged until we click Update plot title.

title: 2  Shiny for Python
text:
2.5 Project structure
The movies app runs, but nothing in the folder tells another developer (or our future selves) which packages it needs or how the editor should be configured. The 02.3_proj-app branch adds these files:
git checkout 02.3_proj-app

pyap/
├── .gitignore
├── .vscode/
│   └── settings.json
├── README.md
├── app.py
├── movies.csv
├── requirements.txt
└── utils.py

The app code (app.py, utils.py, and movies.csv) is unchanged. The branch adds requirements.txt and .vscode/settings.json, and it updates README.md and .gitignore.

2.5.1 requirements.txt
requirements.txt lists the packages the app depends on, one per line:
shiny>=1.2.0
matplotlib>=3.8.0
pandas>=2.1.0
numpy>=1.26.0
Each line sets a minimum version (>=), not an exact one. This makes requirements.txt a looser record than a lockfile: it guarantees a version that’s new enough, but two people installing from it on different days can end up with different versions.8
Anyone who clones the branch can create a virtual environment and install everything in requirements.txt with -r:
uv venv
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -r requirements.txt
If you’re using Python’s built-in venv, the equivalent install command is pip install -r requirements.txt. Once we turn the app into a package, the dependencies will move into pyproject.toml and the exact versions will be recorded in uv.lock (we saw both in the Whole Game chapter, and the Dependencies chapter covers them in detail).


2.5.2 IDE settings
VS Code (and Positron, which is built on the same open source code base) reads project settings from .vscode/settings.json. The settings in this branch are below:
{
    "python.defaultInterpreterPath": ".venv/bin/python",
    "python.terminal.activateEnvironment": true,
    "editor.formatOnSave": true,
    "editor.rulers": [88],
    "[python]": {
        "editor.defaultFormatter": "ms-python.black-formatter"
    }
}
python.defaultInterpreterPath points the editor at the Python inside .venv/, and python.terminal.activateEnvironment activates the virtual environment whenever we open a new terminal. The remaining settings format Python files with Black every time we save, and draw a ruler at 88 characters (Black’s default line length). The Black formatter setting requires the Black Formatter extension.






NoteSharing editor settings



The .gitignore in the earlier branches listed .vscode/, so editor settings were never committed. The 02.3_proj-app branch removes that entry, which means .vscode/settings.json is shared with anyone who clones the repository.

title: 2  Shiny for Python
text:
2.6 Recap
In this chapter we built the app we’ll use throughout the rest of the book, one branch at a time:

02.1_shiny-app: the Old Faithful app introduced the Core API, with a UI object built from ui functions, a server() function with @render outputs, and App() to combine them.
02.2_movies-app: the movies app added dropdown, text, and button inputs, read data from movies.csv, moved the plotting code into scatter_plot() in utils.py, and used @reactive.calc and @reactive.event() to control when the title updates.
02.3_proj-app: the project gained a requirements.txt for its dependencies and a .vscode/settings.json for its editor configuration.

The project is still a folder of loose files, though. The data path depends on the working directory, utils.py is only importable from the same folder, and requirements.txt doesn’t pin exact versions. In the Packages chapter we’ll start turning this project into an installable Python package.

title: 2  Shiny for Python
text:
Python environments are a similar concept to the renv package in R.↩︎
Install uv from the Terminal with: curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh↩︎
The decorated function replaces the output$distPlot <- renderPlot({...}) assignment we’d write in R.↩︎
input.bins() is the Python equivalent of input$bins. The parentheses are easy to forget, especially if you’re used to R.↩︎
App() plays the same role as shinyApp() in R.↩︎
This is the reverse of a named vector in R’s selectInput(), where the names are the labels (c("IMDB rating" = "imdb_rating")).↩︎
Together, these decorators do the same job as eventReactive(input$update_plot_title, ..., ignoreNULL = FALSE) in R.↩︎
requirements.txt fills a role similar to renv.lock, although renv.lock records exact versions and these entries are only lower bounds.↩︎

title: 3  Python Packages
text:
3.1 What is a Python package?
In the Whole Game chapter, a single uv init --package command created a pyproject.toml file, a src/pyap/ folder, and a build system, and we moved on without looking closely at any of them. This chapter slows that step down. We’ll start with the loose files from the end of the Shiny for Python chapter and turn them into an installable package one branch at a time, so each new file has a reason to exist before we add it.
If you’ve read Shiny App-Packages, you’ve seen this conversion before. In R, we added the mandatory fields to DESCRIPTION, configured the .Rproj build tools, and ran usethis::create_package(). The Python version follows the same arc, and I’ll point out where the two languages line up (and where they don’t) along the way.
The diagram below shows the three branches we’ll build in this chapter, starting from the 02.3_proj-app branch:
The first two branches change how the project describes and installs its dependencies, but the app code doesn’t move. Only the last branch turns pyap into a package.
In R, the word “package” covers everything at once. sap is the folder we develop, the thing we install with install.packages(), and the name we pass to library(). Python splits these into three separate ideas, and the documentation uses the word “package” for two of them. I’ve found this is the single biggest source of confusion for R developers reading Python packaging docs, so it’s worth getting the terms straight before we write any files.

title: 3  Python Packages
text:
3.1.1 Modules, packages, and distributions
The Python Packaging User Guide glossary defines the three terms below:

Module: a single .py file. utils.py is a module, and from utils import scatter_plot imports a function from it.
Import package: a folder of modules with an __init__.py file. In the 03.3_create-package branch, src/pyap/ becomes an import package, and the import changes to from pyap.utils import scatter_plot.
Distribution package: the installable archive built from a project (and described by its pyproject.toml). When we run pip install shiny, we’re installing a distribution.

The names of an import package and a distribution package usually match, but they don’t have to. For example, we install scikit-learn with pip install scikit-learn, but we import it with import sklearn. Shiny keeps them the same (pip install shiny and import shiny), and so will pyap.
Distributions come in two formats. A source distribution (or sdist) is a .tar.gz archive of the project’s source files, and a wheel is a pre-built .whl archive that can be installed without a build step.1 We saw both in the dist/ folder at the end of the Whole Game chapter.
By these definitions, the 02.3_proj-app branch holds two modules (app.py and utils.py) and no packages of either kind. By the end of this chapter, it will hold one import package (pyap) that uv can build into a distribution (also pyap).


3.1.2 Anatomy of an app-package
The diagram below maps the files and folders in an R app-package to their Python counterparts. Solid arrows are direct equivalents, and dashed arrows mark mappings that only hold roughly:

        RDir("<code>R/</code>")

        RTests("<code>tests/testthat/</code>")

        RLock("<code>renv.lock</code>")

    end

        PyInit("<code>__init__.py</code>")
        PySrc("<code>src/pyap/</code>")

        PyBuild("build backend<br/>settings")
    end

    RDesc --> PyProj
    RNs -.->|"roughly"| PyInit
    RDir --> PySrc
    RMan -.->|"roughly"| PyDoc
    RTests --> PyTests

    classDef rStyle fill:#2c5282,stroke:#63b3ed,color:#fff

 R app-package (sap) and Python app-package (pyap) 



The ‘rough’ mappings above deserve at least a sentence of explanation (to the best of my knowledge):

NAMESPACE and __init__.py: Python doesn’t have a file that lists exports. Every name in a module is importable unless it starts with an underscore, and __init__.py controls what’s available directly from pyap (along with the optional __all__ list). Imports from other packages are declared in pyproject.toml, not __init__.py.
man/ and docstrings: docstrings live on the objects themselves, so there’s no generated help folder. The Documentation chapter covers them.
inst/ and package data: non-Python files (like movies.csv) can live inside src/pyap/ and be installed with the code. The Data chapter covers how to read them.
.Rbuildignore and build settings: the build backend decides which files go into a distribution, and most backends accept include and exclude settings in a [tool.*] table.

This chapter covers the top row of the diagram (pyproject.toml, __init__.py, and src/pyap/) and the lockfile. The remaining rows have their own chapters.

title: 3  Python Packages
text:
3.2 What is pyproject.toml?
pyproject.toml is the file that tells Python tools what a project is, what it depends on, and how to build it.2 Every modern Python packaging tool reads it, including pip, uv, and the build backends we’ll cover below.






NoteWhy pyproject.toml replaced setup.py





For most of Python’s history, package metadata lived in a setup.py file. setup.py is a Python script that calls setuptools.setup() with the package name, version, and dependencies. Because it’s executable code, tools had to run it to learn anything about the package, and they couldn’t run it without first installing setuptools. A static setup.cfg file was added later, but it only worked with setuptools.
requirements.txt was never a package metadata file at all. It’s a list of packages for pip to install into an environment, which is why we used it in the Shiny for Python chapter. It can’t tell anyone the name or version of our project, and nothing in it describes how to build a distribution.
Three Python Enhancement Proposals (PEPs) replaced these files with a single declarative one:

PEP 518: introduced pyproject.toml and the [build-system] table, so tools know what to install before building a package.
PEP 517: defined a standard interface between installers and build backends, so setuptools became one option among many.
PEP 621: standardized the [project] table for metadata, so any backend reads the name, version, and dependencies from the same place.

You’ll still find setup.py in older projects, and requirements.txt is still common for deployment (we’ll come back to this below). New packages only need pyproject.toml. The Writing your pyproject.toml guide in the Python Packaging User Guide is the canonical reference for the file.




3.2.1 Reading TOML
You don’t have to learn a new configuration language to read pyproject.toml, but it helps to know three rules of TOML (Tom’s Obvious Minimal Language):

A name in square brackets (like [project]) starts a table, and everything below it belongs to that table until the next one starts.
Inside a table, each line is a key = value pair. Strings are quoted, and lists go in square brackets.
A dot in a table name nests it, so [project.scripts] is a table inside [project].

TOML is just a stricter version of the Field: value format in a DESCRIPTION file. The sections below cover the tables we’ll see in this book.


3.2.2 [project]
The [project] table holds the package metadata. The pyproject.toml from the Whole Game chapter is a good example:
[project]
name = "pyap"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "A Shiny for Python app-package"
readme = "README.md"
authors = [
    { name = "Jane Doe", email = "jane.doe@email.io" }
]
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = [
    "matplotlib>=3.11.2",
    "numpy>=2.5.3",
    "shiny>=1.8.0",
]
Only name is strictly required, and version is required unless a tool computes it for us. That’s a much shorter list than the seven mandatory fields in an R DESCRIPTION file.3 requires-python sets the Python versions the package supports, and dependencies lists the distributions it needs at runtime, using the same version specifiers as requirements.txt.


3.2.3 [build-system]
The [build-system] table tells installers which build backend to use and how to install it:
[build-system]
requires = ["uv_build>=0.12.23,<0.13.0"]
build-backend = "uv_build"
requires lists the packages needed to build the project, and build-backend names the object that does the building. We’ll cover backends in their own section below. For now, the important point is what this table signals: a pyproject.toml with a [build-system] table describes something that can be built and installed as a package.


3.2.4 [dependency-groups]
The [dependency-groups] table (PEP 735) holds dependencies we need while developing the package, but that users don’t need to run it:
[dependency-groups]
dev = [
    "pytest>=9.1.1",
]
Dependency groups aren’t included in the package metadata, so installing pyap never installs pytest.4 uv installs the dev group by default when it syncs the project. The Dependencies chapter covers groups in more detail.


3.2.5 [project.scripts]
The [project.scripts] table registers terminal commands that are created when the package is installed. Each key is a command name, and each value points to a function as module:function:
[project.scripts]
pyap = "pyap.app:run"
This is the entry we added in the Whole Game chapter so that typing pyap in a terminal launches the app. R packages don’t have a direct equivalent. We won’t add a launch function in this chapter, and the Launch chapter covers entry points in detail.


3.2.6 [tool.*]
Any table that starts with tool. belongs to a specific tool, and every other tool ignores it. This lets a project keep its configuration in one file instead of a folder of dotfiles. For example, pytest reads its settings from [tool.pytest.ini_options]:
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]
We’ll add [tool.*] tables as we adopt new tools throughout the book. For a real world example of all these tables working together, the pyproject.toml for py-shiny is worth skimming. It’s much longer than ours, but it’s built from the same pieces.






Notepyproject.toml and Posit Connect





rsconnect-python can deploy directly from a pyproject.toml. rsconnect deploy pyproject reads a [tool.rsconnect] table for the app settings:
[tool.rsconnect]
app_mode = "python-shiny"
entrypoint = "app.py"
The [project] dependencies provide the dependency list, and a pinned uv.lock or requirements.txt can be supplied with --requirements-file. Connect Cloud still expects a requirements.txt with app.py as the primary file, so a requirements.txt can come back at deployment time (uv can generate one from uv.lock with uv export). The Deploy section covers both.

title: 3  Python Packages
text:
3.3 Writing pyproject.toml
The first branch replaces requirements.txt with a hand written pyproject.toml. Check out the 03.1_pyproject branch to follow along:
git checkout 03.1_pyproject
The app code doesn’t change. The branch deletes requirements.txt, adds pyproject.toml, and updates the install instructions in README.md:

pyap/
├── .gitignore
├── .vscode/
│   └── settings.json
├── README.md
├── app.py
├── movies.csv
├── pyproject.toml
└── utils.py


3.3.1 Adding project metadata
The full pyproject.toml in this branch is below:
[project]
name = "pyap"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "A Shiny for Python app-package"
readme = "README.md"
authors = [
    { name = "Martin Frigaard" }
]
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = [
    "matplotlib>=3.8.0",
    "numpy>=1.26.0",
    "pandas>=2.1.0",
    "shiny>=1.2.0",
]
The dependencies list holds the same four entries (and lower bounds) as the old requirements.txt, sorted alphabetically. The rest of the table gives the project a name, a version, and a supported Python version, which requirements.txt had no way to record.
The file doesn’t have a [build-system] table yet. This is deliberate. pyap is still a folder of loose modules with nothing to build, so we’re only using pyproject.toml to describe the project and its dependencies.


3.3.2 Installing from pyproject.toml
uv can install the dependencies from a pyproject.toml with the same -r flag we used for requirements.txt:
uv venv
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -r pyproject.toml
If you already have a .venv/ from the earlier branches, you can skip uv venv. The install command only reads the dependencies list. It doesn’t try to install pyap itself (which is good, because there’s nothing to install yet).
We can confirm the environment still works by launching the app the same way as before:
shiny run --reload --launch-browser app.py






TipPositron



Positron watches for pyproject.toml and requirements.txt files. If it finds one in a project that doesn’t have a virtual environment yet, it offers to create one with uv and install the dependencies for us. If uv can’t find a Python installation, the Start Session button also includes an option to install Python with uv.

title: 3  Python Packages
text:
3.4 Managing the project with uv
In the 03.1_pyproject branch, uv is only acting as a faster pip: we create the environment, activate it, and tell it what to install. The 03.2_uv branch hands the whole job to uv’s project commands. uv is also the first option listed on the Shiny for Python install page. Check out the 03.2_uv branch to follow along:
git checkout 03.2_uv
The app code and pyproject.toml are unchanged. The branch adds .python-version and uv.lock, removes both from .gitignore so they’re committed, and updates the commands in README.md:

pyap/
├── .gitignore
├── .python-version
├── .vscode/
│   └── settings.json
├── README.md
├── app.py
├── movies.csv
├── pyproject.toml
├── utils.py
└── uv.lock


3.4.1 Pinning Python
requires-python in pyproject.toml sets the range of Python versions the project supports, but it doesn’t choose one. uv python pin records the exact version uv should use for this project in a .python-version file:
uv python pin 3.12
Returns:

Pinned `.python-version` to `3.12`

The file holds a single line:
3.12
If Python 3.12 isn’t installed, uv downloads it the first time it needs it (we covered uv python install in the Introduction).


3.4.2 Syncing the environment
uv sync reads pyproject.toml, resolves the dependencies, and makes .venv/ match the result:
uv sync

Resolved 45 packages in 127ms
Checked 43 packages in 0.48ms

This one command does the work of the three we ran in the previous branch. uv creates .venv/ if it doesn’t exist (or reuses it if it does), writes uv.lock, and installs the locked versions into the environment. We don’t need to activate the environment first, and we don’t need to tell uv which file to read.






Warninguv sync removes packages



uv sync makes the environment match the lockfile exactly, which means it uninstalls anything that isn’t listed. If you installed extra packages into .venv/ in earlier branches (like polars from the callout in the Shiny for Python chapter), uv sync removes them. From this branch on, add packages with uv add, which updates pyproject.toml, uv.lock, and .venv/ in one step. The Dependencies chapter covers uv add in detail.


To run a command inside the environment, we prefix it with uv run:
uv run shiny run --reload app.py





uv run checks that .venv/ is in sync with uv.lock before running the command, so most of the time we don’t need to call uv sync ourselves.


3.4.3 uv.lock
uv.lock records the exact version of every package in the environment, including the dependencies of our dependencies. pyproject.toml says pandas>=2.1.0, and uv.lock says which pandas was installed. uv writes the lockfile for every platform at once, so a lockfile created on macOS installs the same versions on Windows or Linux.
We don’t edit uv.lock by hand, but it’s worth knowing what’s in it. The diagram below compares how a dependency moves from declaration to installation in R (with renv) and in Python (with uv):





%%{init: {'theme': 'neutral', 'themeVariables': { 'fontFamily': 'monospace', "fontSize":"14px"}}}%%

flowchart TB
    subgraph RDeps["R"]
    direction TB
        RDesc["<code>DESCRIPTION</code><br/><code>Imports</code>"]
        RLib[("project library<br/><code>renv/library/</code>")]
        RLock["<code>renv.lock</code>"]
        RDesc -->|"<code>install_deps()</code>"| RLib
        RLib -->|"<code>renv::snapshot()</code>"| RLock
    end

    subgraph PyDeps["Python"]
    direction TB
        PyProj["<code>pyproject.toml</code><br/><code>dependencies</code>"]
        PyLock["<code>uv.lock</code>"]
        PyVenv[("project environment<br/><code>.venv/</code>")]
        PyProj -->|"<code>uv lock</code>"| PyLock
        PyLock -->|"<code>uv sync</code>"| PyVenv
    end

    classDef rStyle fill:#2c5282,stroke:#63b3ed,color:#fff
    classDef pyStyle fill:#744210,stroke:#f6ad55,color:#fff

    class RDesc,RLib,RLock rStyle
    class PyProj,PyLock,PyVenv pyStyle


 From declared dependency to installed package 



The order of the last two steps is the important difference. renv::snapshot() records whatever is already installed in the project library, so the lockfile follows the environment. uv resolves uv.lock from pyproject.toml first and then installs from it, so the environment follows the lockfile.5 uv sync runs the uv lock step for us whenever pyproject.toml changes.






NoteCommit uv.lock and .python-version



The .gitignore in earlier branches listed .python-version and uv.lock. The 03.2_uv branch removes both entries, so anyone who clones the repository and runs uv sync gets the same Python version and the same package versions we used.




3.4.4 Non-package projects
The pyproject.toml in this branch still doesn’t have a [build-system] table, and uv notices. uv treats a project without a build system as a non-package project: it installs the dependencies into .venv/, but it doesn’t install the project itself.6 The lockfile entry for pyap reflects this with a virtual source (trimmed below):
[[package]]
name = "pyap"
version = "0.1.0"
source = { virtual = "." }
dependencies = [
    { name = "matplotlib" },
    { name = "numpy" },
    { name = "pandas" },
    { name = "shiny" },
]
We can confirm pyap isn’t installed by trying to import it:
uv run python -c "import pyap"

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pyap'

This error is expected. A non-package project is a perfectly good way to manage an app that only ever runs from its own folder, and many Shiny for Python apps never need more. We want pyap to be importable (and testable, and installable), though, so the next step is giving it something to build.

title: 3  Python Packages
text:
3.5 Build backends
A build backend is the tool that turns a project’s source files into a distribution. When an installer like pip or uv needs to build a package, it reads [build-system], installs the packages listed in requires into a temporary environment, and asks the build-backend to produce a wheel or an sdist.7 Installers and backends only talk through the interface defined in PEP 517, so any installer works with any backend.
The [build-system] table for four common backends is below:



Backend
requires
build-backend




uv_build
["uv_build>=0.12.23,<0.13.0"]
"uv_build"


Hatchling
["hatchling"]
"hatchling.build"


setuptools
["setuptools>=61"]
"setuptools.build_meta"


Flit
["flit_core"]
"flit_core.buildapi"



For a pure Python package like pyap, these backends produce nearly the same wheel. They differ in their defaults (where they look for the package, which files they include) and in how much they can be configured. setuptools is the oldest and the one you’ll find in most older projects. Hatchling is the first option in the Python Packaging User Guide tutorial, and Flit is intentionally minimal.
This book uses uv_build, the default backend for uv init --package (it’s the backend in the Whole Game pyproject.toml). It’s built by the same team as uv, it expects the src/ layout we’ll use below, and it needs no configuration for a package like pyap. The version range in requires should match the version of uv you have installed (check it with uv --version), so yours may differ from the one in this chapter.

title: 3  Python Packages
text:
3.6 Creating the package
The 03.3_create-package branch turns pyap into a package. Check it out to follow along:
git checkout 03.3_create-package
The branch makes three changes: it adds a [build-system] table to pyproject.toml, it moves the Python code into src/pyap/, and it updates the import in app.py. The new project structure is below:

pyap/
├── .gitignore
├── .python-version
├── .vscode/
│   └── settings.json
├── README.md
├── movies.csv
├── pyproject.toml
├── src/
│   └── pyap/
│       ├── __init__.py
│       ├── app.py
│       └── utils.py
└── uv.lock

R packages need two things to be packages: a DESCRIPTION file with the mandatory fields and an R/ folder. A Python package needs three: a pyproject.toml with name and version, a [build-system] table, and an import package for the backend to build. We already have the first, so the sections below add the other two.

3.6.1 Adding a build system
We’ll add the [build-system] table to the bottom of pyproject.toml. The complete file is below:
[project]
name = "pyap"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "A Shiny for Python app-package"
readme = "README.md"
authors = [
    { name = "Martin Frigaard" }
]
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = [
    "matplotlib>=3.8.0",
    "numpy>=1.26.0",
    "pandas>=2.1.0",
    "shiny>=1.2.0",
]

[build-system]
requires = ["uv_build>=0.12.23,<0.13.0"]
build-backend = "uv_build"
With this table in place, uv stops treating pyap as a non-package project. It also tells uv_build what to build: by default, uv_build looks for an import package with the same name as the project in src/ (so src/pyap/__init__.py).


3.6.2 Moving the code into src/pyap/
Next, we’ll create the package folder and move both modules into it:
mkdir -p src/pyap
mv app.py utils.py src/pyap/
src/pyap/ needs an __init__.py file to be an import package. Python runs __init__.py the first time pyap is imported, so anything defined or imported in it is available as pyap.<name>. We don’t need to expose anything yet, so the file only holds a docstring describing the package:
"""A Shiny for Python app-package."""
Putting the package under src/ (instead of a pyap/ folder at the project root) means Python can only import pyap after it’s installed, not just because it happens to be in the working directory. The src/ Layout chapter explains why this protects our tests, and the Flat Layout chapter covers the alternative.


3.6.3 Updating imports
app.py imported scatter_plot() with from utils import scatter_plot, which worked because utils.py was in the same folder as app.py. Inside a package, modules import each other using the full package path:
# Run with: uv run shiny run src/pyap/app.py
from shiny import App, ui, render, reactive
import pandas as pd

from pyap.utils import scatter_plot
The rest of app.py (including import pandas as pd) is unchanged, and so is utils.py. pandas, matplotlib, and shiny are installed distributions, so they’re imported by name exactly as before. Only imports of our own code change.






WarningWhy not keep from utils import?



shiny run src/pyap/app.py adds the folder that holds app.py to Python’s search path, so from utils import scatter_plot would still work when we launch the app this way. It breaks as soon as anything imports the app as pyap.app (like a test, or the run_app("pyap.app:app") launch function from the Whole Game chapter), because utils isn’t a top level module. from pyap.utils import scatter_plot works in both cases.




3.6.4 Where the data file goes
movies.csv stays at the project root in this branch. app.py still reads it with pd.read_csv("movies.csv"), and that relative path is resolved from the folder we launch the app from (not the folder that holds app.py). As long as we run the app from the project root, the file is found.
This works, but it’s fragile. The wheel is built from src/pyap/, so movies.csv isn’t part of the installed package, and launching the app from any other folder fails. Moving the file into src/pyap/ doesn’t fix the relative path on its own. The Data chapter moves movies.csv into the package and reads it with importlib.resources, which finds the file wherever the package is installed.


3.6.5 Installing in editable mode
With a build system and an import package in place, uv sync now installs pyap itself along with its dependencies:
uv sync

Resolved 45 packages in 411ms
      Built pyap @ file:///home/path/to/projects/apps/python/pyap                                 
Prepared 1 package in 10ms
Installed 1 package in 0.96ms
 + pyap==0.1.0 (from file:///home/path/to/projects/apps/python/pyap)

uv installs the project in editable mode by default. An editable install points Python at the files in src/pyap/ instead of copying them into .venv/, so changes to the code are picked up the next time pyap is imported (without reinstalling).8 We only need to sync again when pyproject.toml changes. The pyap entry in uv.lock changes from a virtual source to an editable one:
[[package]]
name = "pyap"
version = "0.1.0"
source = { editable = "." }
The import that failed in the previous branch now works, and __file__ shows Python is reading pyap from our source folder:
uv run python -c "import pyap; print(pyap.__file__)"

/path/to/pyap/src/pyap/__init__.py







NoteEditable installs in the Posit docs



The Shiny for Python custom components guide packages its project with a pyproject.toml and installs it with uv pip install -e . during development. The -e flag is the pip style way to request an editable install, and it’s what uv sync does for us automatically in a uv project. The guide points to the Python Packaging User Guide for building and publishing, which we’ll cover in the PyPI chapter.




3.6.6 Running the app
The app now lives at src/pyap/app.py, so we pass that path to shiny run. We’ll run it from the project root, so movies.csv is found:
uv run shiny run --reload --launch-browser src/pyap/app.py
The app looks and behaves exactly as it did in the 02.3_proj-app branch.





We can confirm the package import is working by changing the x axis dropdown and watching the scatter plot update (the plot comes from pyap.utils, so it wouldn’t render if the import failed).

text:
3.7 The development loop
Now that pyap is a package, the day to day loop of editing, documenting, testing, and building looks different from the R workflow. The diagram below maps the devtools functions from the R book to the uv and pytest commands we’ll use in this one:

    end

    subgraph PyLoop["Python (uv + pytest)"]

    end

Two R functions collapse into one Python command. load_all() and install() both become the editable install from uv sync, because the installed package and our source files are the same files. document() disappears, since docstrings don’t need to be rendered into help files before help() can read them. check() doesn’t have a single equivalent; its jobs are split across pytest, linters, and type checkers.
The Development Workflow chapter covers this loop in practice, and the Test Suite and PyPI chapters cover testing and building.

title: 3  Python Packages
text:
3.8 Recap
In this chapter we turned the loose files from the Shiny for Python chapter into an installable package, one branch at a time:

03.1_pyproject: a hand written pyproject.toml with a [project] table replaced requirements.txt, and uv pip install -r pyproject.toml installed the dependencies.
03.2_uv: uv python pin and uv sync handed the environment to uv, which created .python-version, .venv/, and uv.lock. Without a [build-system] table, uv treated pyap as a non-package project and installed only its dependencies.
03.3_create-package: a [build-system] table with uv_build, an import package in src/pyap/, and package imports (from pyap.utils import scatter_plot) made pyap installable, and uv sync installed it in editable mode.

Along the way, we separated modules, import packages, and distributions (which R folds into a single word), and saw why pyproject.toml replaced setup.py, setup.cfg, and requirements.txt. The project still reads movies.csv from the working directory, which we’ll fix in the Data chapter. In the Development Workflow chapter we’ll put the package to work with the edit, sync, and run loop.
For more depth on the topics in this chapter, see:

Python Packages: the Python counterpart to R Packages, 2ed.
Python Packaging User Guide: the official tutorial for building and publishing a package.
uv projects documentation: how uv handles pyproject.toml, uv.lock, and build systems.

title: 3  Python Packages
text:
An sdist is roughly the Python version of a bundled R package (the .tar.gz file from devtools::build()), and a wheel is roughly a binary package.↩︎
pyproject.toml is the closest Python equivalent of the DESCRIPTION file. It also absorbs some of the jobs we’d hand to .Rproj build settings and package configuration in R.↩︎
dependencies plays the role of Imports in DESCRIPTION, and requires-python plays the role of Depends: R (>= 4.1.0).↩︎
[dependency-groups] is roughly the Suggests field, which is where R packages list testthat. The difference is that Suggests is published with the package and dependency groups are not.↩︎
uv sync on a fresh clone is the equivalent of renv::restore().↩︎
uv lets us override this choice with package = true or package = false in a [tool.uv] table, but the [build-system] table is the standard signal.↩︎
R has one build tool built into the language (R CMD build and R CMD INSTALL, which devtools calls for us). Python lets each project choose its own.↩︎
An editable install gives us the same quick feedback loop as devtools::load_all().↩︎

title: 4  Development Workflow
text:
4.1 Running commands in the environment
In the Python Packages chapter, pyap became an installable package, and uv sync installed it into .venv/ in editable mode. This chapter covers what happens after that: the day to day loop of editing code, running the app, and checking the result. Most passes through this loop need no special commands at all. I’ve found the harder part (especially coming from R) is knowing which changes do need one, and which command fixes them.
We’ll use the 04_dev branch for the whole chapter. It builds on 03.3_create-package and adds one lasting change (a light grid on the scatter plot, which we’ll walk through below). The other edits shown are illustrative, so we’ll undo each of those before moving on. If you’re starting fresh, check out the branch and sync the environment:
Every step in the loop (launching the app, opening a Python console, running tests) needs to use the Python inside the .venv/ folder. There are two ways to make sure this happens: 1) prefix each command with uv run, or 2) activate the environment once per terminal session (with source .venv/bin/activate).

title: 4  Development Workflow
text:
4.1.1 With uv run
uv run runs a command inside the project environment without activating it. We’ve used it since the 03.2_uv branch:
uv run shiny run --reload --launch-browser src/pyap/app.py
Before running the command, uv run checks that uv.lock matches pyproject.toml and that .venv/ matches uv.lock, and it updates whichever one is out of date.
I tend to reach for uv run first because it’s hard to run code against a stale environment by accident.
The same prefix works for any command installed in the environment. The first line below opens a Python console, and the second confirms Python is reading pyap from our source folder:
uv run python

Python 3.12.15 (main, Oct  3 2026, 01:03:07) [Clang 22.1.3 ] on linux
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>> 

uv run python -c "import pyap; print(pyap.__file__)"

/home/path/to/pyap/src/pyap/__init__.py



4.1.2 With an activated .venv/
We activated .venv/ in the Shiny for Python chapter, and activation still works in a uv project.
Activating puts the environment’s bin/ folder at the front of the terminal’s PATH, so python, shiny, and (later) pytest resolve to the copies in .venv/:
source .venv/bin/activate
shiny run --reload --launch-browser src/pyap/app.py
Running deactivate returns the terminal to its previous state.






TipOn Windows





On Windows (PowerShell), the activation script is .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1.



The tradeoff is that an activated environment doesn’t check anything. shiny run uses whatever is installed in .venv/ at that moment, so after a change to pyproject.toml or uv.lock, we have to run uv sync ourselves.1


4.1.3 Which should you use?
It’s not necessary to commit to one approach, but it helps to know what each one guarantees. I’ve summarized some of the differences in the table below:




uv run
Activated .venv/




Syncs before running
Yes
No (run uv sync yourself)


Command
uv run shiny run ...
shiny run ...


Scope
One command
The current terminal session


Works in scripts and CI
Yes
Only after activating



I’ll be using uv run in most of the commands in this book, so the examples work in any terminal. Activating is fine for a long interactive session, as long as you remember the uv sync step. Positron activates .venv/ in new terminals for us (we’ll cover this below), so both styles end up available.

title: 4  Development Workflow
text:
4.2 The edit, run, check loop
