title: 4  Development Workflow
text:
4.3 Changes that need ‘No action’
Editing a module in src/pyap/ is the most common change in the loop, and it’s also the simplest. An editable install puts a pointer to our src/ folder into .venv/ instead of a copy of the code (the Python Packages chapter covers the setup). The next time Python imports pyap, it reads our current files.
The pointer is to the folder, not to individual files, so new modules work the same way. If we added a src/pyap/data.py module (as we did in the Whole Game chapter), from pyap.data import ... would work without reinstalling anything.

4.3.1 Reloading the app
The editable install only matters the next time pyap is imported.

--reload is what makes the next import happen right away
shiny run --reload watches the folder that holds app.py and restarts the app whenever a watched file changes

Because app.py and utils.py both live in src/pyap/, saving either one triggers a restart, and the browser tab refreshes itself when the new app is ready.
We can see this with a small edit to scatter_plot() in src/pyap/utils.py. With the app running, we’ll simulate adding a grid to the plot just before the call to plt.tight_layout().





    ax.legend(
        title=col_var.replace("_", " ").title(),
        bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, 1),
        loc="upper left",
    )
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
    plt.tight_layout()
The lines above are already in the 04_dev branch, so if we delete it, save the file, we will watch how the reload happens:





After we saved the file, the terminal showed the app restarting, and the scatter plot in the browser is redrawn with light grid lines.
We didn’t stop the app, reinstall pyap, or refresh the page. This is the one edit in the chapter we keep, and it’s committed on the 04_dev branch.
Each reload restarts the app’s Python process, so every session starts over and any inputs we changed go back to their default values. For an app the size of pyap, this takes a second or two.






NoteWhat --reload watches





By default, --reload only reacts to certain file types (such as .py, .css, .js, and .html files) inside the folder that holds the app. movies.csv fails both tests because it’s a .csv file, and it sits at the project root instead of in src/pyap/.
Running shiny run --help lists the --reload-dir, --reload-includes, and --reload-excludes options for changing what’s watched.

title: 4  Development Workflow
text:
4.4 Changes that need a sync
A sync is needed when a change affects what’s installed in .venv/, rather than the code .venv/ points to. In practice, that means changes to pyproject.toml and uv.lock.

4.4.1 Adding and removing dependencies
uv add and uv remove cover most of these changes. Each one updates pyproject.toml, re-resolves uv.lock, and syncs .venv/ in a single step, so there’s nothing left for us to run afterwards. For example, the commands below add polars (from the callout in the Shiny for Python chapter) and then remove it again:
uv add polars

Resolved 47 packages in 418ms
      Built pyap @ file:///path/to/pyap/                                                         
Prepared 1 package in 10ms
Uninstalled 1 package in 0.86ms
Installed 3 packages in 6ms
 + polars==2.0.0
 + polars-runtime-32==2.0.0
 ~ pyap==0.1.0 (from file:///path/to/pyap)

After uv add, polars appears in the dependencies list with a lower bound, and uv run python -c "import polars" succeeds.
uv remove takes it back out of all three places, so uv.lock is back where it started, and pyproject.toml only differs by whitespace (uv may add a trailing newline when it rewrites the file).
uv remove polars

Resolved 45 packages in 15ms
      Built pyap @ file:///path/to/pyap                                                            
Prepared 1 package in 3ms
Uninstalled 3 packages in 3ms
Installed 1 package in 0.53ms
 - polars==2.0.0
 - polars-runtime-32==2.0.0
 ~ pyap==0.1.0 (from file:///path/to/pyap)

Development tools go in the dev dependency group with --dev, as pytest did in the Whole Game chapter. The Dependencies chapter covers version constraints, groups, and upgrades.


4.4.2 Editing pyproject.toml by hand
Editing pyproject.toml directly (instead of with uv add) leaves uv.lock and .venv/ behind until something syncs them. uv run catches up on the next command, but an activated environment won’t.
The package version is a good example, because Python reads it from metadata written at install time, not from pyproject.toml. With the environment activated, we can print the installed version with importlib.metadata:
source .venv/bin/activate
python -c "from importlib.metadata import version; print(version('pyap'))"

0.1.0

Next, we’ll make another illustrative edit and change version = "0.1.0" to version = "0.1.1" in pyproject.toml.
[project]
name = "pyap"
1version = "0.1.1"
description = "A Shiny for Python app-package"
readme = "README.md"
authors = [
    { name = "Martin Frigaard" }
]
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = [
    "matplotlib>=3.8.0",
    "numpy>=1.26.0",
    "pandas>=2.1.0",
    "shiny>=1.2.0",
]

[build-system]
requires = ["uv_build>=0.12.23,<0.13.0"]
build-backend = "uv_build"

1

Change from “0.1.0” to “0.1.1”


Running the same command still prints 0.1.0. The editable install points at our code, but the package metadata is a snapshot from the last sync. uv sync rebuilds it:
uv sync

Resolved 45 packages in 522ms
      Built pyap @ file:///path/to/pyap                            
Prepared 1 package in 9ms
Uninstalled 1 package in 0.69ms
Installed 1 package in 0.80ms
 - pyap==0.1.0 (from file:///path/to/pyap)
 + pyap==0.1.1 (from file:///path/to/pyap)

python -c "from importlib.metadata import version; print(version('pyap'))"

0.1.1

uv run python -c "..." would have printed 0.1.1 without the explicit uv sync, because uv run syncs first. We’ll undo the edit (along with the lockfile change the sync made) and sync again:
git restore pyproject.toml uv.lock
uv sync

Resolved 45 packages in 1ms
      Built pyap @ file:///path/to/pyap                            
Prepared 1 package in 4ms
Uninstalled 1 package in 0.25ms
Installed 1 package in 0.79ms
 - pyap==0.1.1 (from file:///path/to/pyap)
 + pyap==0.1.0 (from file:///path/to/pyap)

The same rule applies to the rest of [project] (such as requires-python, dependencies, and the [project.scripts] commands we’ll add in the Launch chapter), and to the [build-system] table. All of them are read when the package is installed, so a change only takes effect after a sync.


4.4.3 Switching branches
Each pyap branch carries its own pyproject.toml and uv.lock, but .venv/ isn’t tracked by Git, so it stays put when we switch branches. After a git checkout, a git pull, or a fresh clone, uv sync brings .venv/ in line with whatever the branch declares (and the next uv run does the same thing on its own).


4.4.4 uv lock and uv sync
uv sync runs uv lock for us whenever pyproject.toml has changed, so we rarely need uv lock by itself. It’s useful when we want to update the lockfile without touching .venv/, such as confirming that a hand edit to pyproject.toml still resolves:
uv lock

title: 4  Development Workflow
text:
4.5 Changes that need a restart
The editable install keeps .venv/ pointed at our current code, and a sync keeps the installed packages current, and neither changes the code the Python processes have already imported. Python imports each module once per process and caches it, so a running process keeps the version it loaded until it’s restarted (or told to reload).
shiny run --reload handles this for the app by restarting the process on every save. There are two exceptions to this: commands in the Python console, and basically anything the app reads only when it starts.

4.5.1 The Python console
The Console is where the editable install feels the least like load_all().2 Suppose we import scatter_plot() into a console (uv run python, started from the project root) to try it outside of the app. Note–the Python session is the one loaded from .venv/bin/python*:
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> from pyap import utils
>>> movies = pd.read_csv("movies.csv")
>>> fig = utils.scatter_plot(movies, "critics_score", "audience_score", "mpaa_rating", 0.4, 3)





If we now edit utils.py and call utils.scatter_plot() again, we get the old version. Running from pyap import utils again doesn’t help, because Python finds pyap.utils in its module cache and never opens the file.
We have two options. The first is importlib.reload(), which re-executes a module that’s already been imported:
>>> import importlib
>>> importlib.reload(utils)

<module 'pyap.utils' from '/path/to/pyap/src/pyap/utils.py'>

The second is restarting the console and running the imports again. I’ve found restarting is the more reliable habit, for the reasons in the warning below.






WarningThe limits of importlib.reload()





importlib.reload() is useful for quick checks, but it misses changes in a few common situations:

One module at a time: reloading pyap.utils doesn’t reload the modules it imports, and reloading pyap doesn’t reload pyap.utils.
Names imported with from: after from pyap.utils import scatter_plot, the name scatter_plot still points to the old function until we run the from import again.
Third party packages: if uv add or uv sync upgrades a package the console has already imported (like pandas), restart the console.










NoteIPython autoreload





IPython (the enhanced console behind Positron’s Python console) includes an autoreload extension that reloads changed modules before each command:
%load_ext autoreload
%autoreload 2
This is convenient for long console sessions, but it can still miss the same edge cases as importlib.reload(). When the results don’t make sense, restart.





4.5.2 Data and running apps
app.py reads movies.csv once, when the module is imported. Editing movies.csv doesn’t trigger --reload (see the note above), so the app keeps showing the old data until it restarts.
If we make changes to movies.csv, we have to press Ctrl + C in the terminal, then run the app again to pick up the change. The Data chapter moves the file into the package.
The same is true after hands edit to pyproject.toml while the app is running. --reload doesn’t watch pyproject.toml, so we’d have to stop the app and restart it with uv run, which syncs before launching.
If we launch an app started without --reload, we need to restart after every change.

title: 4  Development Workflow
text:
4.6 Running tests
Tests close the loop. pytest starts a new Python process each time it runs, so it always imports the current code in src/pyap/ and nothing needs reloading. With the uv run prefix, it also runs against a synced environment:
uv run pytest

=================== test session starts ===================
platform linux -- Python 3.12.3, pytest-9.1.0, pluggy-1.6.0
rootdir: /path/to/pyap
configfile: pyproject.toml
plugins: shiny-1.6.3, anyio-4.14.0
collected 0 items

=================== no tests ran in 0.00s ===================

The 04_dev branch doesn’t have a tests/ folder yet, and pytest isn’t installed in this branch’s environment, so the command above has nothing to run here.3 We added both in the Whole Game chapter (uv add --dev pytest and a tests/test_data.py file), and the Test Suite chapter adds them to pyap.
Once tests exist, two variations are worth knowing during development:

Run a single test file:4

uv run pytest tests/test_data.py

Stop at the first failure

uv run pytest -x
The Tests section covers fixtures, testing modules, and system tests, starting with the Test Suite chapter.

title: 4  Development Workflow
text:
4.7 Using Positron for the loop
Positron isn’t required to run any of the commands I’ve covered so far (every step above is a Terminal command). However, Positron puts the same steps into panes that share a single environment, which removes a few of the places where things can drift out of sync. Below I’ll cover some of the other Positron settings for Python package development.

4.7.1 Choosing an interpreter
The .vscode/settings.json file from the 02.3_proj-app branch sets python.defaultInterpreterPath to .venv/bin/python. Positron will also detect .venv/ folders in the project on its own.
The interpreter picker in the top right corner of the window should show the Python from .venv/; if it doesn’t, select it there.





If .venv/ didn’t exist when the project was opened, run uv sync in the terminal first, then select the new environment.
With .venv/ selected, the console, the editor, and the test runner all use the same environment as uv run.


4.7.2 The console
The Python console starts in the project folder, so the pd.read_csv("movies.csv") example above works without changing directories. The restart button in the Console pane’s toolbar starts a fresh session, which is the restart from the previous section.
The console behaves like an activated environment: it doesn’t sync anything. After a hand edit to pyproject.toml, run uv sync in the terminal and then restart the console.


4.7.3 The terminal
The python.terminal.activateEnvironment setting in .vscode/settings.json activates .venv/ in every new terminal, so the prompt starts with (pyap).





Both styles from the start of this chapter work there:
uv run shiny run ...
and …
shiny run ...
launch the same app.


4.7.4 Running the app
When src/pyap/app.py is open in the editor, the Run Shiny App button (from the Shiny extension) launches the app with reloading turned on and displays it in the Viewer pane. Saving app.py or utils.py restarts the app, exactly as --reload does in the terminal.
app.py still reads movies.csv with a relative path, though, so the app only finds the file when it’s launched from the project root. If the app fails with a FileNotFoundError, launch it from the terminal instead:
uv run shiny run --reload --launch-browser src/pyap/app.py
The Data chapter removes this dependence on the working directory.

title: 4  Development Workflow
text:
4.9 Recap
In this chapter we walked through the development loop for pyap on the 04_dev branch:

uv run runs a command in .venv/ and syncs the environment first. An activated .venv/ works too, but we have to run uv sync ourselves.
Edits to Python code in src/pyap/ need no action, because the editable install points .venv/ at our source files. shiny run --reload restarts the app whenever we save.
Changes to dependencies or metadata need a sync. uv add and uv remove sync for us, a hand edit to pyproject.toml or a new branch needs uv sync (or the next uv run), and uv lock updates only the lockfile.
Code a process has already imported needs a restart. In the console, that means restarting (or importlib.reload() for quick checks), and data read at startup means restarting the app.

Tests run in a fresh process with uv run pytest, and Positron ties the console, terminal, and app runner to the same .venv/. In the next section of the book, starting with the Documentation chapter, we’ll use this loop to add documentation, dependencies, data, and a launch function to pyap.

text:
What’s ahead
Documentation covers writing docstrings for the functions in pyap and generating HTML documentation from them with pdoc, mkdocs, or great-docs. In R, roxygen2 comments are rendered into help files with document(); Python reads docstrings directly, so the work is mostly in writing them well.
Dependencies covers declaring, pinning, and managing the packages pyap depends on in pyproject.toml, and keeping environments reproducible across machines with uv add, uv lock, and uv sync.

By the end of this section, pyap will be a self contained app-package: documented, reproducible, carrying its own data and assets, and launchable from the command line. The Debugging and Testing sections build on this foundation.

title: 5  Documentation
text:
5.1 What is a docstring?
In the Development Workflow chapter, we settled into a loop of editing code in src/pyap/, saving, and checking the result. pyap installs and runs, but its only documentation is a single sentence on scatter_plot() and another in __init__.py. Anyone opening the package (including us, six months from now) has to read the function body to learn what each argument expects and what comes back. This chapter fixes that by writing complete docstrings for the code in pyap, then rendering them into an HTML documentation site.
If you’ve read the Documentation chapter of Shiny App-Packages, you’ve done this before with roxygen2. In R, we wrote #' comments above each function and ran devtools::document() to turn them into .Rd files in man/. Python skips the build step: a docstring is stored on the function itself, so help() can read it the moment the module is imported. I’ve found this shifts the work from running tools to writing well, so most of this chapter is about what goes inside the triple quotes.
A docstring is a string literal placed as the first statement in a module, function, or class. Python doesn’t discard it like a comment. It attaches the string to the object as its __doc__ attribute, which is what makes docstrings readable from the console, the editor, and documentation tools.
scatter_plot() in the 04_dev branch already has a one line docstring:
A comment in the same position (# Create a scatter plot...) would look almost identical in the editor, but it would be invisible to everything below.

title: 5  Documentation
text:
def scatter_plot(df, x_var, y_var, col_var, alpha_var, size_var, title=""):
    """Create a scatter plot of df colored by a categorical variable."""


5.1.1 Where Python reads docstrings
The fastest way to read a docstring is help() in a Python console. We’ll start one from the project root with uv run python and import the function:
>>> from pyap.utils import scatter_plot
>>> help(scatter_plot)

Help on function scatter_plot in module pyap.utils:

scatter_plot(df, x_var, y_var, col_var, alpha_var, size_var, title='')
    Create a scatter plot of df colored by a categorical variable.

help() prints the function’s signature above the docstring, so the arguments and their defaults come for free.1 In a terminal, the output opens in a pager; press q to return to the prompt.
The raw string is available on the __doc__ attribute:
>>> scatter_plot.__doc__

'Create a scatter plot of df colored by a categorical variable.'

Modules and packages have docstrings too. pyap.__doc__ returns the sentence in src/pyap/__init__.py from the Python Packages chapter, and help(pyap) lists the package docstring along with its contents.
Editors read docstrings as well. In Positron, hovering over scatter_plot in app.py shows its signature and docstring in a tooltip, and the same text appears in the signature help while we type the arguments.

The diagram below shows the two routes a docstring takes from our source files to a reader:

    end

The top route imports pyap and reads __doc__ from the live objects. help() works this way, and so does pdoc, which we’ll use to build the HTML site. The bottom route parses the .py files without running them. Editors typically use a language server for hover text, and mkdocstrings (a plugin for mkdocs) reads source files by default. The difference matters for pyap, because importing pyap.app runs code (we’ll come back to this when we build the site).
Every route reads the same string. There’s no generated help folder to keep in sync, so the docstring in the source file is the documentation.

│   └── pyap/
│       ├── __init__.py
│       ├── app.py
│       └── utils.py
└── uv.lock

No files are added to the package. Documentation in Python lives inside the files we already have, which is why the tree looks exactly like the one from the 04_dev branch.

5.2.1 PEP 257 basics
PEP 257 sets the ground rules every docstring convention builds on. The ones we’ll follow in pyap are:

Use triple double quotes ("""), even for one line docstrings.
Start with a one line summary that fits on the first line and ends with a period. PEP 257 recommends the imperative mood (“Create a scatter plot”, not “Creates a scatter plot”).
For longer docstrings, leave a blank line after the summary, then add the details. Put the closing """ on a line by itself.
Place the docstring as the first statement in the body (or at the top of the file, for a module docstring).

The existing docstring on scatter_plot() already follows the first two rules. The summary line deserves extra care, because it’s the line tools show in package indexes and tooltips. PEP 257 doesn’t say anything about how to describe arguments or return values, though. That job belongs to a docstring convention.


5.2.2 Choosing a convention
A docstring convention is just an agreed set of section headings and layouts, so people and tools know where to find the parameters, the return value, and the examples.2 The two most common conventions in data science code are below:

NumPy style: section titles underlined with dashes, and each parameter on its own line followed by its type.
Google style: section titles followed by a colon (Args:, Returns:), with each parameter indented beneath.

The Whole Game chapter used Google style for geyser_waiting(), and it’s a fine choice. For pyap, I recommend NumPy style. pandas, numpy, and matplotlib (all three of the packages scatter_plot() depends on) document their functions this way, so our help pages will read like the ones we consult while writing the code. NumPy style also has more room for longer descriptions, which helps when an argument needs a sentence or two of explanation.
The convention matters less than consistency. Pick one for the whole package, and tell the documentation tools which one you picked (we’ll do this with a flag below).


5.2.3 Documenting scatter_plot()
A NumPy style function docstring has a summary line, an extended description, and a series of sections. The full docstring for scatter_plot() is below:
def scatter_plot(df, x_var, y_var, col_var, alpha_var, size_var, title=""):
    """Create a scatter plot colored by a categorical variable.

    Draws one scatter layer per category in `col_var`, so each category
    gets its own color and legend entry. Axis labels and the legend title
    are built from the column names (underscores become spaces, and each
    word is capitalized).

    Parameters
    ----------
    df : pandas.DataFrame
        Data containing the columns named in `x_var`, `y_var`, and
        `col_var`.
    x_var : str
        Name of the numeric column mapped to the x axis.
    y_var : str
        Name of the numeric column mapped to the y axis.
    col_var : str
        Name of the categorical column used to color the points. Rows
        with a missing value in this column are not plotted.
    alpha_var : float
        Point transparency, from 0 (transparent) to 1 (opaque).
    size_var : float
        Point size. The marker area is `size_var ** 2 * 10`.
    title : str, optional
        Plot title. The default (an empty string) leaves the plot
        untitled.

    Returns
    -------
    matplotlib.figure.Figure
        The figure holding the scatter plot.

    Notes
    -----
    Colors come from the matplotlib `tab10` colormap, which repeats
    after ten categories.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import pandas as pd
    >>> from pyap.utils import scatter_plot
    >>> movies = pd.read_csv("movies.csv")
    >>> fig = scatter_plot(movies, "critics_score", "audience_score",
    ...                    "mpaa_rating", 0.4, 3)
    """
Each section maps to something a reader would otherwise have to work out from the code:

Parameters: one entry per argument, written as name : type with the description indented below it. Optional arguments add optional after the type.
Returns: the type of the returned object (and a short description). scatter_plot() returns the figure rather than drawing it, which is what @render.plot expects.
Notes: details that don’t belong to a single argument. The tab10 limit is easy to miss until a column has more than ten categories.
Examples: code a reader can paste into the console, written in the >>> prompt format.3

I’ve written the descriptions from the reader’s side of the function. col_var doesn’t just say “column for color”; it also says what happens to missing values, because that’s the question someone debugging a sparse plot will have. This is the same advice I gave for @param in the R book: include the type and what the argument does.






TipTypes in docstrings and type hints





NumPy style puts each parameter’s type in the docstring. Python also supports type hints in the function signature (def scatter_plot(df: pd.DataFrame, x_var: str, ...)), and many documentation tools display both. We’ll keep the types in the docstring for now, so the signature in utils.py doesn’t change in this chapter.





5.2.4 Module docstrings
A module docstring describes the file as a whole. It must be the first statement in the file, above the imports. The complete src/pyap/utils.py is below (the function body is unchanged from the 04_dev branch):


show/hide src/pyap/utils.py
"""Plotting utilities for the pyap movies app.

The functions in this module are plain matplotlib code with no Shiny
dependencies, so they can be called from the app, from a test, or from
the Python console.
"""

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd


def scatter_plot(df, x_var, y_var, col_var, alpha_var, size_var, title=""):
    """Create a scatter plot colored by a categorical variable.

    Draws one scatter layer per category in `col_var`, so each category
    gets its own color and legend entry. Axis labels and the legend title
    are built from the column names (underscores become spaces, and each
    word is capitalized).

    Parameters
    ----------
    df : pandas.DataFrame
        Data containing the columns named in `x_var`, `y_var`, and
        `col_var`.
    x_var : str
        Name of the numeric column mapped to the x axis.
    y_var : str
        Name of the numeric column mapped to the y axis.
    col_var : str
        Name of the categorical column used to color the points. Rows
        with a missing value in this column are not plotted.
    alpha_var : float
        Point transparency, from 0 (transparent) to 1 (opaque).
    size_var : float
        Point size. The marker area is `size_var ** 2 * 10`.
    title : str, optional
        Plot title. The default (an empty string) leaves the plot
        untitled.

    Returns
    -------
    matplotlib.figure.Figure
        The figure holding the scatter plot.

    Notes
    -----
    Colors come from the matplotlib `tab10` colormap, which repeats
    after ten categories.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import pandas as pd
    >>> from pyap.utils import scatter_plot
    >>> movies = pd.read_csv("movies.csv")
    >>> fig = scatter_plot(movies, "critics_score", "audience_score",
    ...                    "mpaa_rating", 0.4, 3)
    """
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()

    categories = sorted(df[col_var].dropna().unique())
    cmap = plt.get_cmap("tab10")

    for i, cat in enumerate(categories):
        subset = df[df[col_var] == cat]
        ax.scatter(
            subset[x_var],
            subset[y_var],
            alpha=alpha_var,
            s=size_var ** 2 * 10,
            color=cmap(i % 10),
            label=str(cat),
        )

    ax.set_xlabel(x_var.replace("_", " ").title())
    ax.set_ylabel(y_var.replace("_", " ").title())
    if title:
        ax.set_title(title)
    ax.legend(
        title=col_var.replace("_", " ").title(),
        bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, 1),
        loc="upper left",
    )
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
    plt.tight_layout()

    return fig


src/pyap/app.py gets a module docstring too. The # Run with: comment can stay on the first line, because comments aren’t statements; the docstring is still the first statement in the file:
# Run with: uv run shiny run src/pyap/app.py
"""Shiny app for exploring the movies data.

Defines the UI (`app_ui`), the server function (`server()`), and the
`app` object that `shiny run` looks for. The data are read from
`movies.csv` in the working directory when this module is imported.
"""

from shiny import App, ui, render, reactive
import pandas as pd

from pyap.utils import scatter_plot
The last sentence is a deliberate warning. Reading movies.csv at import time is the behavior that will trip up pdoc below, and the docstring is the right place to tell readers about it until the Data chapter changes it.
The server() function also gets a short docstring. Shiny passes it three objects, so the Parameters section names their types and lists the inputs and outputs the function uses:
def server(input, output, session):
    """Server logic for the movies app.

    Parameters
    ----------
    input : shiny.Inputs
        Input values from the sidebar (`x`, `y`, `z`, `alpha`, `size`,
        `plot_title`, and `update_plot_title`).
    output : shiny.Outputs
        Outputs rendered by the app (`scatterplot`).
    session : shiny.Session
        The current user session.
    """
The rest of app.py is unchanged. The functions defined inside server() (new_plot_title() and scatterplot()) are created each time a session starts, so documentation tools don’t see them; the existing comment above new_plot_title() is the right level of documentation for them.


5.2.5 The package docstring
The docstring in src/pyap/__init__.py is the first thing a reader sees in help(pyap) and on the front page of a documentation site. We’ll keep the summary line from the Python Packages chapter and add a short description that points to the modules:
"""A Shiny for Python app-package.

`pyap` packages the movies review app as an installable Python package.
The app (UI, server, and the `app` object) lives in `pyap.app`, and the
plotting code it calls lives in `pyap.utils`.
"""
A package docstring is a good place for orientation, not detail. The function level docstrings carry the specifics, and the package docstring tells the reader where to look for them.4


5.2.6 Confirming the docstrings
Docstrings are part of the source code, so the editable install picks them up without a sync (this is the No action path from the Development Workflow chapter). A console that already imported pyap.utils still holds the old function, though, so we’ll restart it (or start a new one with uv run python) and call help() again:
>>> from pyap.utils import scatter_plot
>>> help(scatter_plot)

The output should show the full NumPy style docstring below the signature. help() prints the sections as plain text; the underlined headings are what documentation tools look for when they turn the docstring into HTML.

title: 5  Documentation
text:
5.3 Rendering documentation to HTML
help() and editor tooltips cover anyone who already has pyap installed. A documentation site covers everyone else (and makes the docstrings searchable). We’ll use pdoc in the 05_document branch, then look briefly at two alternatives.

5.3.1 Adding pdoc
pdoc generates API documentation from a package’s docstrings with no configuration file. We only need it while developing pyap, so we’ll add it to the dev dependency group with --dev:
uv add --dev pdoc

uv add updates pyproject.toml, uv.lock, and .venv/ in one step. The new table in pyproject.toml is below:

[dependency-groups]
dev = [
    "pdoc>=X.Y.Z",
]
Installing pyap never installs pdoc, because dependency groups aren’t part of the package metadata (we covered this in the Python Packages chapter).


5.3.2 Previewing the site
pdoc takes the name of the package to document. With uv run, we’re sure it imports the editable install of pyap from .venv/:
uv run pdoc --docformat numpy pyap

This starts a local web server and opens the documentation in the browser. The --docformat numpy flag tells pdoc to read the Parameters, Returns, Notes, and Examples sections as NumPy style (without it, the underlined headings render as plain text). The package docstring becomes the landing page, and pyap.app and pyap.utils each get their own page. Press Ctrl + C in the terminal to stop the server.

pdoc only documents public names. Anything that starts with an underscore is skipped, and if a module defines __all__, only the names it lists are included.5






Warningpdoc imports pyap



pdoc builds its pages from the imported package (the top route in the diagram above), and importing pyap.app runs pd.read_csv("movies.csv"). The relative path is resolved from the folder we run pdoc in, so pdoc has to be run from the project root, exactly like the app. From any other folder, the import of pyap.app fails with a FileNotFoundError. The Data chapter removes this dependence on the working directory.




5.3.3 Writing a static site
To write the site to files instead of serving it, we pass an output folder with -o:
uv run pdoc --docformat numpy -o docs pyap
pdoc writes one HTML page per module, plus an index page and a search index. The docs/ folder should look like this:


docs/
├── index.html
├── pyap/
│   ├── app.html
│   └── utils.html
├── pyap.html
└── search.js

The pages are self contained, so opening docs/index.html in a browser shows the same site as the preview. The 05_document branch lists docs/ in .gitignore, because the HTML can always be rebuilt from the docstrings. We’ll publish it in the Deploy section.


5.3.4 mkdocs with mkdocstrings
mkdocs builds a documentation site from a folder of Markdown files, and the mkdocstrings plugin inserts API documentation from docstrings into those pages. It takes more setup than pdoc, but it’s the better fit when the site needs written guides alongside the reference pages. mkdocs isn’t part of the 05_document branch, so treat this section as a sketch.
Both packages go in the dev group (the [python] extra installs the Python handler for mkdocstrings):
uv add --dev mkdocs "mkdocstrings[python]"
The site is configured in an mkdocs.yml file at the project root. The settings below tell mkdocstrings to look for code in src/ and to read NumPy style docstrings:
site_name: pyap
plugins:
  - search
  - mkdocstrings:
      handlers:
        python:
          paths: [src]
          options:
            docstring_style: numpy
The pages live in a docs/ folder. A docs/index.md file with the line below renders the documentation for pyap.utils:
::: pyap.utils
uv run mkdocs serve previews the site, and uv run mkdocs build writes it to a site/ folder. mkdocstrings reads the source files by default (the bottom route in the diagram), so it doesn’t need movies.csv to be found.






Notedocs/ means different things





pdoc -o docs writes generated HTML into docs/, and mkdocs reads Markdown sources from docs/. Don’t use both tools with the same folder. If you switch pyap to mkdocs, point pdoc somewhere else (or drop it).





5.3.5 great-docs
great-docs builds Quarto based documentation sites for Python packages. If you’ve built an R package site with pkgdown, or a book like this one with Quarto, it’s the most familiar of the three. A later chapter covers great-docs in more depth.


5.3.6 Which should you use?
You don’t have to choose a documentation site generator before writing docstrings, but it helps to know what each one asks of us. The table below summarizes the three tools:










pdoc
mkdocs + mkdocstrings
great-docs

Covered in a later chapter

Quarto based site


Reads docstrings by
Importing the package
Parsing source files (by default)
Covered in a later chapter



I’ll use pdoc for the rest of this section, because a package with two modules needs a reference, not a website. When pyap grows (or needs tutorials alongside the API reference), the docstrings we wrote in this chapter carry over unchanged, because every tool reads the same strings.

5.4 Comparing documentation with R
The Python Packages chapter mapped document() to “docstrings (no build step)”. The table below fills in the rest of that comparison:

Python (pyap)

The build step is the biggest difference. In R, documentation can go stale: we can edit a roxygen2 block and forget to run document(), which is why the R book covers roxygen2::needs_roxygenize(). In Python, there’s nothing to forget at the help file level. The HTML site is the only generated output, and it’s rebuilt from the docstrings whenever we run pdoc.
The tradeoff is that Python has no single standard for the inside of a docstring. roxygen2 defines one set of tags for every R package, while Python leaves the format to conventions like NumPy and Google style. Choosing one (and telling the tools about it) is the step R doesn’t need.

title: 5  Documentation
text:
5.5 Recap
In this chapter we documented pyap on the 05_document branch:

Docstrings are strings stored on Python objects as __doc__. help() and pdoc read them from the imported package, and editors and mkdocstrings read them from the source files.
PEP 257 sets the basic shape (triple quotes, a one line summary in the imperative mood, a blank line, then details), and a convention sets the sections. We used NumPy style to match pandas, numpy, and matplotlib.
scatter_plot() and server() got full docstrings, utils.py and app.py got module docstrings, and __init__.py got a package docstring that points readers to both modules.
uv add --dev pdoc added pdoc to the dev group, and uv run pdoc --docformat numpy pyap previews the site (-o docs writes it to files). mkdocs with mkdocstrings and great-docs are alternatives for larger sites.

pdoc also exposed the same problem the app has: importing pyap.app only works from the project root, because movies.csv is read from the working directory. In the next chapter, Dependencies, we’ll take a closer look at how pyap declares and locks the packages it needs, before the Data chapter moves movies.csv into the package.
For more depth on the topics in this chapter, see:

PEP 257: the docstring conventions every style builds on.
numpydoc style guide: the full list of NumPy style sections.
pdoc documentation: command line options, templates, and docstring formats.
mkdocstrings Python handler: configuration for mkdocs sites.

help(scatter_plot) is the Python version of ?scatter_plot. The difference is that ? reads an .Rd file generated by document(), and help() reads the string attached to the function.↩︎
Conventions play the role of roxygen2 tags. @param becomes a Parameters section, @return becomes Returns, and @examples becomes Examples.↩︎
The >>> format comes from Python’s doctest module, and pytest can run these examples as tests with the --doctest-modules flag. The example above reads movies.csv from the working directory, so it only runs from the project root (the Data chapter removes this limitation).↩︎
The package docstring is the Python counterpart of the package level help page (?sap) that usethis::use_package_doc() creates with the "_PACKAGE" sentinel.↩︎
This is the closest pdoc comes to @export. In R, unexported functions still get help pages unless they’re marked @noRd; in Python, a leading underscore keeps a function out of the generated site.↩︎
